facts.text: On this date in 1960, the first televised U.S. presidential debate aired. Kennedy wore makeup; Nixon refused. Radio listeners thought Nixon won. TV viewers handed Kennedy the election.
On this date in 1687, a Venetian mortar shell hit the Parthenon—which the Ottomans were using as a gunpowder magazine. The explosion that destroyed it happened 2,000 years after it was built.
More people live inside a circle drawn 4,000 km around Bangladesh than outside it. That single radius captures over half of humanity.
Canada has more lakes than every other country combined—roughly 879,000 of them. It holds about 20% of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water.
Manila is the most densely populated city on Earth, with over 71,000 people per square kilometer—denser than any neighborhood in New York or Tokyo.
On this date in 1929, the London stock market began its collapse one month before Wall Street's crash — the British panic helped trigger the American one, not the other way around.
The NYSE was founded under a buttonwood tree in 1792, but the famous Buttonwood Agreement had only 24 signatories — fewer people than a typical office meeting room holds today.
On September 26, 2008, Washington Mutual was seized by regulators — the largest bank failure in U.S. history, with $307B in assets, handled so quietly that markets barely moved the next morning.
Saudi Aramco briefly held a $2 trillion valuation in 2019, making it worth more than the entire GDP of Italy — a country of 60 million people with 2,000 years of economic history.
The S&P 500 has historically risen in the final quarter of the year about 75% of the time, making Q4 the most reliably bullish stretch on the calendar by a wide margin.

On this date in 1983, Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov ignored his own nuclear early-warning system showing five incoming US missiles — correctly judging it a glitch. His unauthorized calm prevented a retaliatory launch.
On this date in 2003, NASA's SMART-1 spacecraft left Earth powered entirely by an ion thruster, accelerating by expelling xenon atoms one by one. It took 13 months to reach the Moon.

Your skeleton is not the rigid frame it appears — bone is a living tissue that completely replaces itself roughly every decade, continuously dissolving and rebuilding in response to the loads you place on it.

A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere roughly 20 kilometers across, making its surface gravity 200 billion times stronger than Earth's — enough to flatten a mountain into a film one atom thick.

Mantis shrimp see with 16 types of color receptors compared to the human three, yet research shows they are actually worse at distinguishing similar hues — their eyes solve color by timing signals, not mixing them.

On this date in 1960, Nixon and Kennedy held the first televised presidential debate. Radio listeners thought Nixon won. Television viewers handed it to Kennedy. The medium had become the message overnight.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. Oxford dates to 1096; Tenochtitlán wasn't founded until 1325.
On this date in 1687, a Venetian mortar shell struck the Parthenon — which the Ottomans were using as a gunpowder magazine. It had stood intact for 2,100 years and was destroyed in seconds.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She died in 30 BC; the pyramid was finished around 2560 BC.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — 33 years before Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone. The world had fax before it had phone calls.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in 2012, it spread so fast it feels ancient.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home that may never have existed. Untranslatable — English borrowed the feeling without ever finding the word.
On this day in 1888, T.S. Eliot was born. He gave us 'objective correlative' — the idea that art works by finding objects, not words, to carry emotion.
Acedia (n.): a Greek monastic term for spiritual torpor, the noonday demon of listlessness. Medieval monks feared it more than pride. We renamed it depression.
On this date in 1983, the Oxford English Dictionary completed its first full revision in 70 years. 'Serendipity,' coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, made the final cut unchanged.
On this date in 2017, China's central bank declared all ICOs illegal, triggering a 40% Bitcoin price drop in 72 hours — then the market fully recovered within six weeks.
On this date in 2022, Ethereum completed The Merge, switching from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake and cutting the network's energy consumption by approximately 99.95%.
Bitcoin's smallest unit, the satoshi, wasn't named in Satoshi Nakamoto's whitepaper — the term was coined by forum users in 2010 and only later became canonical.
The DAO hack in 2016 didn't exploit a flaw in Ethereum itself — it exploited a reentrancy bug in a third-party smart contract, yet Ethereum still hard-forked to reverse it.
Satoshi Nakamoto's genesis block contains the headline 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — a timestamp and an editorial, permanently encoded in the chain.
On this date in 2015, Google DeepMind published the Nature paper on Deep Q-Networks beating human performance on 49 Atari games — widely credited as the opening shot of the modern deep RL era.
On this date in 2022, the US Commerce Department added 31 Chinese AI entities to its export control list, marking the first time AI chip access became explicit foreign-policy leverage.
The entire GPT-3 training run consumed roughly 1,300 MWh — about what 120 average US homes use in a year. A single model, once.
RLHF was described in a 1992 paper by Benbrahim and Franklin on robot locomotion. OpenAI did not invent it; they industrialized it at a scale its authors never imagined.
AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins before most structural biology labs had processed their hundredth. The entire prior experimental database took 50 years to build.
